Chapter 7: The Shadow Side of Denial—Violence, Scapegoating, and the Need for Enemies
You know, sometimes the fear of death doesn’t just stay hidden inside—it spills out into the world and shapes the way we interact with each other. When people feel threatened, or when their sense of meaning gets shaken up, there's this almost instinctive urge to look for someone to blame. That need for security, for a clear sense of “us” versus “them,” can get pretty intense.
Picture a community facing tough times—maybe it’s economic struggles, sudden social changes, or a crisis that turns old certainties upside down. Tension starts to build. Suspicion creeps in. For many, it feels easier to point fingers than to face the uncomfortable truth that life is unpredictable and fragile. And when leaders sense this anxiety, they might rally folks around a common enemy, promising safety and order.
It’s a pattern we’ve seen play out over and over again throughout history. Groups often end up defining themselves by what—or who—they oppose, instead of just what they stand for. Scapegoating becomes a way to manage fear, a way to turn anxious energy into action. The “other”—whether it’s someone from a different religion, race, or who thinks differently—suddenly becomes the symbol of everything that feels threatening.
The thing is, most of us don’t even notice just how much our need for security shapes our attitudes. The desire to fit in, to belong, to feel safe, can so easily tip over into excluding others, sometimes even fueling violence. When we deny the reality of death, and project that fear outward, it doesn’t just stay personal—it can become a powerful force for division.
And sometimes, it’s subtle. Maybe it’s a rivalry at work, a disagreement between neighbors, or a heated political debate. Suddenly, these everyday moments become battlegrounds for much deeper fears. The urge to be right, to defend what you believe, can drown out empathy and understanding. Underneath it all, that unspoken fear of mortality finds its voice in anger and hostility.
But here’s the thing: sometimes, something shifts. A simple act of kindness, a moment of shared laughter, or just taking the time to really listen—these small gestures can break the pattern. Suddenly, the boundaries start to dissolve, and we remember what we have in common. It becomes obvious that the real enemy isn’t the “other” at all—it’s the fear that drives us apart.
The real challenge is to notice how denial shapes more than just individual choices—it shapes entire societies. Most of us don’t realize how deeply our need for certainty and belonging can lead us to exclude others. So, the task becomes this: face fear honestly, build bridges instead of walls, and look for security in compassion, not division.
